title: PostgreSQL: transactions & concurrency control
description: Why a transaction alone is not enough, and how row-level locking, serializable isolation and optimistic concurrency solve the auction-bid race.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: Two users bid on the same auction at the same time, each in its own Read Committed transaction that reads max bid then inserts. What can go wrong?

options.text: Both read the same old max, so a losing bid can still be inserted.
options.why: Right: the check and the write are not atomic across transactions.

options.text: PostgreSQL always blocks the second transaction until the first ends.
options.why: Plain reads do not block each other.

options.text: Both bids are rejected, which is the safest outcome.
options.why: Neither is rejected automatically.

options.text: The database merges the two bids into a single row.
options.why: No merging happens.

questions.explanation: Saying "we use transactions" is not enough. Explain how the check and the write become one atomic decision.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE do in the bidding transaction?

options.text: Locks the auction row so other writers wait until this transaction ends.
options.why: Right: serialises bidders on that row.

options.text: Makes the row read-only for everyone permanently.
options.why: The lock lasts only until commit or rollback.

options.text: Copies the row into a backup table.
options.why: No copy is made.

options.text: Raises the isolation level for the whole database.
options.why: It affects specific rows in this transaction only.

questions.explanation: Lock the row you are making a decision about. Mention it explicitly instead of only saying "transaction".

questions.prompt: When is row-level locking preferable to SERIALIZABLE isolation?

options.text: When you know exactly which rows need atomic updates and conflicts are limited to them.
options.why: Right: lower overhead and no retries needed.

options.text: When the logic spans many tables and it is unclear what to lock.
options.why: That favours Serializable.

options.text: When you want the database to retry conflicting work for you.
options.why: Neither retries automatically; Serializable needs app retries.

options.text: When you want to avoid thinking about concurrency at all.
options.why: Locking requires you to think; Serializable is the easier-to-write option.

questions.explanation: Use locks for targeted cases like bids or inventory; Serializable for complex multi-table logic.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of using Serializable instead of row locks?

options.text: Lower concurrency, more tracking overhead and transactions that must retry on conflict.
options.why: Right: simple to write, costly under contention.

options.text: It silently produces wrong results under load in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It is the safest level; the cost is aborts, not anomalies.

options.text: It stops working when replicas are present under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Replication does not disable it.

options.text: It permanently locks entire tables.
options.why: It uses predicate tracking, not whole-table locks.

questions.explanation: The trade-off table: Serializable is easy to reason about but scales less well when conflicts are frequent.

questions.prompt: What failure mode must code that uses explicit row locks handle?

options.text: Deadlocks, where two transactions wait on each other's locks.
options.why: Right: PostgreSQL aborts one so the other can proceed.

options.text: Serialization failures that require full retries in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That is the Serializable cost, not the locking cost.

options.text: Phantom writes created by replicas.
options.why: Replicas do not take part in locking.

options.text: Index corruption caused by waiting transactions without any extra configuration.
options.why: Waiting does not corrupt indexes.

questions.explanation: Lock rows in a consistent order and be ready to retry if the database picks your transaction as the deadlock victim.

questions.prompt: You add a version column and run UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = 5. Zero rows are updated. What does it mean?

options.text: Someone else changed the row first, so re-read and retry.
options.why: Right: that is optimistic concurrency control.

options.text: The row does not exist anymore and the table is corrupt in a typical production setup.
options.why: It only means the version no longer matched.

options.text: The database is out of memory and rejected the update.
options.why: That would raise an error, not update zero rows.

options.text: The update succeeded but a replica will apply it later.
options.why: Zero rows means nothing was changed.

questions.explanation: OCC avoids holding locks and works best when conflicts are rare.

questions.prompt: True or false: optimistic concurrency control works best when conflicts are rare, and badly when many transactions constantly collide on the same rows.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: rare conflicts keep retries cheap.

options.text: False
options.why: It is the opposite; heavy contention wastes work on retries.

questions.explanation: Frequent conflicts mean many retries and wasted work, so pessimistic locking or a different design fits better there.

questions.prompt: True or false: saying "we use PostgreSQL because it is ACID" is enough, without explaining how you will use transactions and locks.

options.text: True
options.why: It is too vague for most interviewers.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: show how you will achieve the consistency.

questions.explanation: Explain the mechanism: which transaction, which locks or isolation level, and what retry behavior.

questions.prompt: Which approach avoids lost updates on a counter such as stock = stock - 1?

options.text: A single atomic UPDATE using the current value in the statement itself.
options.why: Right: the database applies it atomically per row.

options.text: Read the value in the app, subtract one and write it back for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Two instances can read the same value and overwrite each other.

options.text: Cache the value in the app and write it hourly.
options.why: Stale caches break correctness.

options.text: Use two separate transactions to read then write under normal operating conditions.
options.why: The gap between them is where the race happens.

questions.explanation: Push the arithmetic into the statement, or lock the row first, so the read and write are one step.
